source.title: Revisiting Optimism and Model Complexity in the Wake of Overparameterized Machine Learning
source.authors: Pratik V. Patil; Jin-Hong Du; R. Tibshirani

record.file_problem: The full paper is present and readable. Some mathematical symbols are corrupted by text extraction, but this does not prevent identifying the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses different model classes and a random-X prediction-error measure to report double-descent results and to examine how the curve relates to an alternative complexity measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports double-descent outcomes for ridgeless regression, random forests, and random-feature regression. Figure 8 varies sample size for optimally tuned predictors, but does not report a result about increasing data near the interpolation threshold. No epochs are swept. References to double descent in other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study's own simulations show double descent in random-X prediction error for ridgeless regression, random-feature regression and random forests (V4). It re-plots the same error against a proposed effective complexity measure, random-X degrees of freedom, which falls past the interpolation threshold (V7). The methods differ from both originals, though the random-forest setup follows Belkin et al.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that raw parameter count and classical fixed-X df are inadequate for overparameterized models, since any interpolator gets df = n. They propose emergent and intrinsic random-X df, which distinguish interpolators and allow comparison across model classes. Under this measure, interpolators past the threshold become less complex as size grows.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates regression and random-forest simulations using random-X prediction error and random-X degrees of freedom; it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments.
record.problems: The double-descent curves are reported in figures rather than numeric tables. Although the experiments average over stated repetitions, no uncertainty estimates are stated. The evidence is from simulated regression and random-forest settings, not deep networks.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 8 varies sample size for optimally tuned predictors, but the text does not report a result about more data raising error near interpolation. It is therefore not recorded as a claim-bearing row.

untested.parts: Figure 8 varies n only for optimally tuned predictors; there is no sample-wise test near interpolation.
No test that one measure predicts peak location across size, epochs and samples.
Label noise, multiple peaks, and peak removal under optimal regularization are not examined.
kNN and lasso along λ are not capacity sweeps past interpolation. No classification tasks.

missing.what: Random forest: emergent and intrinsic random-X df decrease after the interpolation threshold, and error is re-plotted against random-X df. This bears on V7.
missing.locator: Section 6.2; Figure 6 middle and right panels

missing.what: Asymptotic ridgeless regression (n=400): error versus p/n, with the text noting prediction error blows up at γ=1 while df is maximized at γ=1 and decreases beyond it; error is also plotted against df.
Lassoless (minimum ℓ1 interpolator) regression versus p/n: df is maximized at γ=1 and decreases beyond it; error is plotted against df.
Random features: error plotted against random-X df.

record.verdict_notes: The V4 and V7 evidence is figure-based, from simulations averaged over 500 repetitions with no uncertainty shown. The V7 support is an interpretive re-plotting: the text never states that the curve becomes U-shaped. It is closely related to Curth et al. 2023, which the paper cites.

versions.untested_parts: No training-epoch or training-time sweep is reported.
The sample-size experiment concerns optimally tuned predictors and does not test whether more data raises test error near an interpolation threshold.
The reported settings do not establish the curve across all model classes or settings.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Noise level, multiple or split peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization are not tested as causes or conditions of the peak.
The comparison of prediction error against random-X degrees of freedom is shown for the ridgeless-regression illustration, not across all model classes or axes.
